title: The Real Presence
hook: Catholics teach bread and wine become Christ's body and blood; the Orthodox affirm the change and call it mystery

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism, deeper: new birth itself, or its sign and seal. Your line was born of water. Did the water at the sink remind you of a beginning? Day one thousand one hundred one.

"This is an hard saying; who can hear it?" Many of his own disciples say it in the sixth chapter of John, in a synagogue in Capernaum, and they have a point. Jesus has just told the crowd that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood, they have no life in them. Readers still argue over how he meant it. John says that from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Then Jesus turns to the twelve: "Will ye also go away?" Peter answers for them, and it's an honest answer: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." He doesn't claim to understand. He stays. Today's word: transubstantiation.

Fast forward to the night before he died. Jesus takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and says, in the King James: "Take, eat; this is my body." Then the cup: "this is my blood." Paul, writing to Corinth, asks: "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" What does "is" mean at that table? That question will take two days. Today, two churches that answer: really, truly is. Catholics teach that at the consecration in the Mass, the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. Transubstantiation is the word Catholic councils used to name that change. It borrows an old distinction from philosophy: what a thing really is, its substance, and how it appears to the senses. The appearances of bread and wine remain: the taste, the color, the crumbs. But what it is has changed. That's why Catholics kneel or bow before the consecrated host, keep it in a tabernacle, and sit before it in silent adoration. Orthodox Christians also confess that the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood. But Orthodox teaching is wary of defining how. In the Divine Liturgy the change is prayed for: the priest asks the Holy Spirit to come down on the gifts. Orthodox Christians call the sacraments mysteries, and they're content to leave this one there. A change, really. Explained, not fully. These two traditions describe the same table in different ways, and each holds its way with reverence. Tomorrow, other churches' views of the table. Today, notice Peter again. He didn't say, now I understand. He said, to whom shall we go? In John's telling, faith can look like staying with words you can't fully explain.
screen: `THIS IS MY BODY.` · `CATHOLIC: SUBSTANCE CHANGED.` · `APPEARANCES OF BREAD REMAIN.` · `ORTHODOX: A REAL CHANGE, A MYSTERY.` · then, large: `TO WHOM SHALL WE GO?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow to a mystery. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind something in your life you can't fully explain and can't quite dismiss: a love, a grief, a moment that felt larger than itself, or, if you receive communion, the bread and the cup. Don't try to solve it. Just let it be bigger than your explanation of it. If it feels right, bow your head slightly, the way people do at the altar, a small gesture that says I don't have this figured out. If you pray, you can offer that bow to God. If you don't, let it simply be respect. The bell holds the time.
Transubstantiation. The Catholic word for bread and wine becoming Christ's body and blood, while their appearances remain.
Your line: a holy mystery. Today, when something won't fit your explanation, try staying with it a little longer before you walk away. Day one thousand one hundred one.

howItsDone: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, bow or kneel before the consecrated host, and keep it in a tabernacle for adoration; Orthodox Christians receive the holy gifts in the Divine Liturgy, confessing a real change and calling it a mystery.

fork.setup: you're Peter. crowds are walking away over a hard saying, and Jesus asks if you'll go too. what do you say?
fork.reveal: Peter doesn't claim to understand: "to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." he stays.

original.note: Greek: a mystery — the Orthodox word for a sacrament.

trapdoor: what you thought: transubstantiation means the bread turns into flesh you can see.
what it means: in Catholic teaching, what the bread and wine are becomes Christ's body and blood, while how they look and taste stays the same.
what a scholar hears: substance and appearances. the Catechism names a change of substance, not of appearances; the Orthodox affirm the change and decline to define how.

notes: 'many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him' paraphrases John 6:66 without quotation marks; 'many' is the text's word.
Catholic summary: substance/appearances (accidents) distinction; 'the word Catholic councils used' refers to Lateran IV and Trent without dates. Confirm.

Orthodox summary: real change affirmed; reluctance to define the manner; epiclesis in the Divine Liturgy. Some Orthodox confessions have used the Greek equivalent of transubstantiation; 'slow to explain how' is meant to allow for that. Confirm fairness.
Lutheran, Reformed and memorial views reserved for day 1102.
Trapdoor: Latin derivation trans + substantia stated in games only; confirm.

Editor pass: removed the narrator's claim that Jesus 'doesn't say, I meant it as a picture' (it takes a side the churches dispute, cf. John 6:63, and tomorrow covers) and the matching 'softened his words' myth item; Orthodox reticence stated fairly; closing line attributed to John's telling; cut the trans/substantia etymology from the trapdoor.

Audit (2026-10-02): John 6:60 says 'many ... of his disciples', not 'the disciples' (the twelve stay), so the hook and match now say so; 'the word ... used to name how' changed to 'name that change' (Trent calls the change itself transubstantiation); the closing line no longer places John 6 at a table, since it is set in the Capernaum synagogue.
